newsitem.title: UK: Dlr regains poise after drop on Thai baht float.
newsitem.headline: Dlr regains poise after drop on Thai baht float.

text.p: The dollar was regaining the upper hand against the yen in Europe's morning after being sold off during Asian trade following the flotation of the Thai baht.

Overnight there was a rush to buy up the yen, which had gained something of a safe-haven status after the Bank of Thailand said it was dropping its pegged rates system against a basket of currencies and allowing the market to set exchange rates.
As a result the dollar sank to its session low of 114.15 yen, although it had recovered to 114.55/60 by 0740 GMT as the surprise from the baht flotation wore off.
But it was still below its European closing level of 114.79/84 yen on Tuesday.

The Thai baht, meanwhile, had steadied after falling to a record low of 29.00 to the dollar in the offshore market on news of the float. It was at 28.300/900 at 0750 GMT compared with 24.25 just before the news.

"Whenever a developing currency is allowed to float, there is always some fear in the market and that causes a capital outflow, and in the Asian region the safe haven is obviously the yen," said Alessandra Stagliano, economist at Daiwa Europe. "But this isn't going to have lasting consequences (for the yen)."
But even after the initial safe-haven rush to the yen ends, the Thai baht flotation may have more fundamental consequences which would be yen-positive, analysts said.

"The fact Thailand has floated its currency could be the prelude to more countries moving, which would provide support for the yen, although that will take time to feed through," said Gerard Lyons, chief economist at DKB International.

Since Thailand had delinked its currency from a basket dominated by the U.S. dollar, it may be forced to readjust its foreign reserves from dollars to more regional currencies, and the yen was an obvious one, analysts said.

Events in Asia had taken the market's attention off the U.S., where the Federal Open Market Committee was holding a two-day meeting which ends today. However, the market had not been expecting the Fed to move rates.

"We don't see anything happening that might jolt the dollar out of its current range. There's no major influence coming from the FOMC, and everybody seems comfortable with the dollar's recent range," Daiwa's Stagliano said.
DKB's Lyons said that as far as US-based factors were concerned, the U.S. non-farm payrolls data, due out on Thursday, were likely of more interest to the market.

Against the mark, the dollar was below the 40-month high of 1.7488 marks it reached on Tuesday, but it was firming in European morning trade. Dollar/mark was at 1.7449/52 against 1.7408/18 in late European trade on Tuesday.

Late on Tuesday, Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer said he believed the current strength of the dollar was due more to a correction from recent weakness and did not reflect expectations for a weak euro when European monetary union takes place.
Elsewhere, the market was looking at the British budget due out this afternoon, with the market expecting a net tightening of four billion pounds.

Sterling was at 2.8955/65 marks after closing in Europe at 2.8875/85 on Tuesday. Sterling/mark had risen to a five-year high of 2.9100 yesterday but had dropped later in the day as nervousness began to permeate the market ahead of the UK budget and because of soft UK economic data.
Cable was at $1.6576/86 against its late Tuesday level of $1.6575/80.
